en: Hi, how are you?
note: The idiom uses kuulua (to be heard). Answer with a partitive adjective: Hyvää. / Ihan hyvää.

en: Fine, thanks — and you?
note: sinulle is the allative (-lle) of sinä. Puhekieli shortens sinulle → sulle.

en: Nice to meet you, I'm Ishtiak.
note: tutustua = to get acquainted. Use hauska tavata when you have met briefly before.

en: Hello! Long time no see.
note: Fixed elative expression (pitkä → pitkästä). Terve is casual but works with anyone your own age.

en: Good morning! Did you sleep well?
note: Greetings take the partitive: hyvää huomenta, hyvää päivää, hyvää iltaa.

en: Sorry, am I disturbing you?
note: The question clitic -ko/-kö attaches to the verb. häiritä takes a partitive object.

en: Thanks for the help, it helped a lot.
pu: Kiitti avusta, se autto tosi paljon.
note: kiitos + elative (-sta/-stä). apu → avusta shows consonant gradation p → v.

fi: Ei kestä, ei se ollut mitään.
en: You're welcome, it was nothing.
pu: Ei kestä, ei se ollu mitään.
lit: Not lasts, not it was anything-PART.
note: Ei kestä literally 'it doesn't last' = no trouble. mitään is the partitive of mikään in a negative clause.

en: Have a good weekend! See you on Monday.
note: Weekdays take the essive (-na/-nä) for 'on Monday'. Nähdään is a passive form used as 'see you'.

en: Same to you, have a nice evening.
note: Wishes are partitive because the verb toivon ('I wish') is left out.

fi: Kuinka päiväsi on mennyt tähän mennessä?
en: How has your day gone so far?
pu: Miten sun päivä on menny tähän mennessä?
lit: How day-your has gone this-to by?
note: päiväsi uses the possessive suffix -si. Puhekieli replaces it with sun + bare noun.

fi: Pitkä päivä takana, olen aivan poikki.
en: Long day behind me, I'm completely worn out.
pu: Pitkä päivä takana, oon ihan poikki.
lit: Long day behind, am completely broken.
note: olla poikki = to be exhausted. Very common everyday idiom.

en: Nice to see you again.
note: nähdä takes a partitive object for people. Puhekieli drops the d: nähdä → nähä.

en: Bye, I have to go now.
pu: Moi moi, mun täytyy mennä nyt.
note: täytyy is a necessive verb: the subject goes in the genitive (minun, sinun, hänen).

en: Welcome to our place, come further in.
note: meille = allative of me. peremmälle is a fixed invitation to step inside.

en: Thanks for the invitation, I'll gladly come.
note: mielellään ('gladly') inflects with the person: mielelläni, mielelläsi, mielellään.

en: Could you repeat that? I didn't hear properly.
note: Negative past = en + past participle (kuullut). Puhekieli drops the final -t: kuullu.

fi: Puhutko englantia? Suomeni on vielä heikkoa.
en: Do you speak English? My Finnish is still weak.
pu: Puhuksä englantii? Mun suomi on vielä heikkoo.
lit: Speak-you-Q English-PART? Finnish-my is still weak-PART.
note: Languages are partitive objects with puhua. The complement heikkoa is partitive because 'Finnish' is treated as a mass.

en: Could you speak a little more slowly, please?
note: Comparative adverb: hitaasti → hitaammin. The most useful sentence a learner owns.

en: Fun that we ran into each other here.
note: Spoken Finnish uses the passive (törmättiin) for 'we'. että often shortens to et.

en: I'm originally from Bangladesh.
note: kotoisin + elative (-sta/-stä) is the standard way to state your origin.

fi: Asun Helsingissä, mutta olen syntynyt Turussa.
en: I live in Helsinki, but I was born in Turku.
pu: Mä asun Helsingissä, mut oon syntyny Turus.
lit: Live-I Helsinki-in, but am born Turku-in.
note: Place names take the inessive (-ssa/-ssä) here. Helsinki → Helsingissä shows k → g gradation.

en: I'm twenty-eight years old.
note: After a number, the noun is singular partitive: vuotta, not vuosia. Alternative: Olen 28-vuotias.

fi: Puhun bengalia, englantia ja vähän suomea.
en: I speak Bengali, English and a little Finnish.
pu: Mä puhun bengalii, englantii ja vähän suomee.
lit: Speak-I Bengali-PART, English-PART and a-little Finnish-PART.
note: Puhekieli often turns the partitive -a into a long vowel: suomea → suomee.

en: I've lived in Finland for three years.
pu: Mä oon asunu Suomes kolme vuotta.
note: Perfect tense = olla + -nut/-nyt participle. Duration takes the bare accusative/partitive: kolme vuotta.

en: What is your name?
note: Written Finnish doubles the possession (sinun + -si). Speech keeps only sun.

en: How is your name spelled?
note: Passive present -taan/-tään. Very handy at a counter or reception desk.

en: I moved to Finland because of work.
note: X:n takia = 'because of X' and requires the genitive. duuni is very common slang for work.

fi: Olen naimisissa ja meillä on kaksi lasta.
en: I'm married and we have two children.
pu: Mä oon naimisis ja meil on kaks lasta.
lit: Am in-marriage and at-us is two child-PART.
note: Possession = adessive (-lla/-llä) + on. lapsi → lasta after a number.

en: I'm not married yet.
note: Negation verb ei conjugates (en, et, ei, emme, ette, eivät) while the main verb stays in the stem.

en: I work as a nurse at the central hospital.
note: Professions take the essive (-na/-nä) with 'work as'.

en: I study information technology at a university of applied sciences.
note: opiskella takes a partitive object. amk is the everyday short form.

en: Which part of Finland are you from?
note: mistä päin is more natural than plain mistä when asking about a region.

en: I'm interested in Finnish culture.
note: kiinnostunut governs the elative (-sta/-stä) on both adjective and noun.

en: My address is Koulukatu 12 B.
note: osoite → osoitteeni; the stem doubles the t before a possessive suffix.

en: My email address is on that card.
note: tuossa (inessive of tuo) shortens to tos in speech.

en: My date of birth is the third of March.
note: Dates: ordinal + month in the partitive. Speech uses synttärit for the birthday itself.

en: I have a residence permit and a personal identity code.
note: hetu is the universal abbreviation for henkilötunnus in Finland.

en: I'm here on holiday, not for work.
pu: Mä oon täällä lomalla, en duunissa.
note: State expressions: lomalla (adessive) but töissä (inessive plural). These are fixed.

en: Tell me a bit about yourself.
note: kertoa + elative for the topic. itse inflects: itsestäni, itsestäsi, itsestään.

fi: Minulla on kaksi veljeä ja yksi sisko.
en: I have two brothers and one sister.
pu: Mul on kaks veljee ja yks sisko.
lit: At-me is two brother-PART and one sister.
note: Numbers above one force the singular partitive: veljeä, not veljet.

en: My parents still live in my home country.
pu: Mun vanhemmat asuu vielä mun kotimaassa.
note: Spoken Finnish uses the 3rd person singular verb for plural subjects: asuvat → asuu.

en: My wife comes home at six.
note: Clock times take the ablative (-lta/-ltä): kuudelta, seitsemältä.

fi: Poikani on kolmevuotias ja tosi vilkas.
en: My son is three years old and really lively.
pu: Mun poika on kolmevuotias ja tosi vilkas.
lit: Son-my is three-year-old and really lively.
note: Compound age adjective: numeral + vuotias, written as one word.

en: My daughter starts school next autumn.
pu: Mun tytär aloittaa koulun ens syksynä.
note: Seasons with ensi take the essive: ensi syksynä, ensi keväänä.

en: We visit grandma's place every summer.
note: In speech, 'we' + verb becomes me + passive: käymme → me käydään.

en: My cousin is getting married next month.
pu: Mun serkku menee naimisiin ens kuussa.
note: mennä naimisiin uses the illative plural — motion into the state of marriage.

fi: Isäni on ollut eläkkeellä jo kaksi vuotta.
en: My father has been retired for two years already.
pu: Mun isä on ollu eläkkeel jo kaks vuotta.
lit: Father-my has been retirement-on already two years-PART.
note: olla eläkkeellä = to be retired (adessive of eläke). Duration: kaksi vuotta.

en: Our family is quite big.
note: aika before an adjective means 'quite/fairly', not 'time'.

en: I call my mother every Sunday.
note: soittaa + allative for the person you call. äiti → äidille (t → d gradation).

en: I get along well with my parents-in-law.
pu: Mä tuun hyvin toimeen appivanhempien kaa.
lit: Come-I well by with parents-in-law-my with.
note: tulla toimeen jonkun kanssa = to get along with someone. kanssa → kaa in speech.

fi: Meillä on ollut pieni riita, mutta se on jo ohi.
en: We've had a small argument, but it's over already.
pu: Meil on ollu pieni riita, mut se on jo ohi.
lit: At-us has been small quarrel, but it is already past.
note: Existential perfect: meillä on ollut. The complement stays nominative here.

en: The children are at their grandparents'.
note: luona ('at someone's place') is a postposition and needs the genitive before it.

en: My husband always helps with the housework.
note: mies → mieheni. Housework activities take the inessive plural: kotitöissä.

en: We have a dog called Rekku.
note: nimeltä (ablative of nimi) is the fixed way to say 'called/named'.

fi: Olen ollut yhdessä tyttöystäväni kanssa neljä vuotta.
en: I've been together with my girlfriend for four years.
pu: Mä oon ollu mun tyttöystävän kaa neljä vuotta.
lit: Am been together girlfriend-my with four years-PART.
note: olla yhdessä jonkun kanssa. Duration is expressed with a bare partitive: neljä vuotta.

en: The relatives are coming to visit at Christmas.
note: tulla kylään = to come visiting. Holidays take the essive: jouluna, juhannuksena.

en: Who is looking after the children in the evening?
note: hoitaa takes a partitive object for ongoing care. illalla = adessive of ilta.

fi: Meidän pitäisi käydä useammin katsomassa heitä.
en: We should go and see them more often.
pu: Meidän pitäis käydä useemmin kattomassa niitä.
lit: Our should to-go more-often watching them-PART.
note: pitäisi = conditional necessive; the subject is genitive. käydä + -massa = go do something.

en: Congratulations on your wedding day!
note: onnea is partitive (a wish). X:n johdosta = on the occasion of X.

en: I live on the upper floor of a two-bedroom flat.
note: Finnish flats are counted by rooms: yksiö, kaksio, kolmio (1, 2, 3 rooms including the living room).

en: The rent is eight hundred euros a month.
note: After a numeral, euro stays singular partitive: euroa. kuukaudessa shortens to kuussa.

en: Are water and electricity included in the rent?
note: sisältyä + illative. In speech people usually say kuuluuko … vuokraan.

en: The kitchen is small but functional.
note: mutta reduces to mut in nearly all speech.

en: The washing machine is in the bathroom.
note: kylppäri is the everyday slang for kylpyhuone.

fi: Meidän taloyhtiössä on oma sauna ja pyykkitupa.
en: Our housing company has its own sauna and laundry room.
pu: Meidän taloyhtiös on oma sauna ja pyykkitupa.
lit: Our house-company-in is own sauna and laundry-room.
note: taloyhtiö is the housing cooperative — a word you meet constantly when renting in Finland.

en: Can you close the window? There's a draught in here.
note: vetää used impersonally means 'there's a draught'. Total object ikkunan for a completed action.

en: I have to clean the living room today.
note: olkkari = colloquial olohuone. pitää is more common than täytyy in speech.

en: I'll take the rubbish out in the evening.
note: roskat is always plural. Present tense covers the near future in Finnish.

en: The tap is leaking, I should call the maintenance man.
note: soittaa + allative for the person called. Conditional pitäisi softens the statement.

en: The flat has good ventilation.
note: Inessive + on is how Finnish says 'X has' for places and things.

en: The sofa doesn't fit in this room.
note: mahtua + illative. Speech drops the ht cluster: mahtua → mahtuu → mahu in some dialects.

fi: Muutamme uuteen asuntoon ensi kuun alussa.
en: We're moving to a new flat at the beginning of next month.
pu: Me muutetaan uuteen asuntoon ens kuun alussa.
lit: Move-we new-into flat-into next month-of beginning-in.
note: Adjective and noun both take the illative. Note the passive for 'we' in speech.

en: Where are the keys?
note: In speech, plural subjects take the singular verb on.

en: I left the keys inside.
note: sisälle is a directional form (to the inside); sisällä would be static.

fi: Naapuri pitää kovaa meteliä myöhään illalla.
en: The neighbour makes a lot of noise late in the evening.
pu: Naapuri pitää kovaa meteliä myöhään illal.
lit: Neighbour keeps loud-PART noise-PART late evening-on.
note: pitää melua = to make noise. Partitive object because the noise is ongoing.

en: The heating isn't working properly.
note: Essential sentence for a Finnish winter. kunnolla = properly, adverb from kunto.

en: I put the laundry out to dry on the balcony.
note: The third infinitive illative (-maan) expresses purpose after laittaa.

fi: Ovi on lukossa, minulla ei ole avainta.
en: The door is locked, I don't have a key.
pu: Ovi on lukos, mul ei oo avainta.
lit: Door is lock-in, at-me not is key-PART.
note: In a negative existential, the object becomes partitive: avain → avainta.

fi: Sopimus on voimassa vuoden loppuun asti.
en: The contract is valid until the end of the year.
pu: Sopimus on voimas vuoden loppuun asti.
lit: Contract is force-in year-of end-into until.
note: olla voimassa = to be in force. X:n loppuun asti = until the end of X.

en: I usually wake up at half past six.
note: Finnish counts half toward the coming hour: puoli seitsemän = 6:30, not 7:30.

en: I take a shower before breakfast.
note: käydä suihkussa (inessive) = to take a shower. ennen governs the partitive.

fi: Juon aina kaksi kuppia kahvia aamulla.
en: I always drink two cups of coffee in the morning.
pu: Mä juon aina kaks kuppii kahvii aamul.
lit: Drink-I always two cup-PART coffee-PART morning-on.
note: Double partitive: numeral forces kuppia, and the substance kahvia is partitive too.

en: I leave for work at eight.
note: töihin is the illative plural of työ. Speech: lähden → lähen.

en: The trip takes about twenty minutes.
note: kaksikymmentä → kakskyt in fast speech; minuutti → minsa is slang.

en: I eat lunch around midday.
note: syödä takes a partitive object when the eating is unfinished/ongoing.

en: I take a short break around two.
pu: Mä pidän pienen tauon kahen aikaan.
note: pitää tauko = to take a break. X:n aikaan = around X o'clock.

en: I stop by the shop on the way home.
note: käydä = to go somewhere and come back, distinct from mennä.

en: We cook together in the evening.
note: tehdä ruokaa = to cook. Partitive object because cooking is a process.

en: I watch the news at eight o'clock.
note: uutiset is always plural. katson → katon is standard puhekieli.

en: Before going to bed I read a little.
note: ennen + partitive. nukkumaanmeno is a noun built from the verb phrase.

en: I go to bed around eleven.
note: mennä nukkumaan uses the -maan infinitive. menen → meen in speech.

en: I usually sleep seven hours.
note: Numeral + singular partitive again: tuntia, not tunteja.

en: On weekends I sleep in longer.
note: The -isin suffix means 'habitually on': aamuisin, iltaisin, viikonloppuisin.

en: The alarm clock rings too early.
note: soida = to ring/sound (intransitive), as opposed to soittaa = to play/call.

en: I hit the snooze button twice more.
note: kahdesti / kolmesti = twice / three times, a compact alternative to kaksi kertaa.

en: I brush my teeth in the morning and in the evening.
pu: Mä pesen hampaat aamul ja illal.
note: Finnish does not add 'my' — body parts belong to the subject by default.

fi: Arki on aika kiireistä näinä päivinä.
en: Everyday life is quite hectic these days.
pu: Arki on aika kiireistä näinä päivinä.
lit: Weekday-life is quite busy-PART these-as days-as.
note: arki (weekday life) is a core Finnish concept, opposed to pyhä/vapaa.

en: I try to keep a regular daily rhythm.
note: Total object (-n) because keeping the rhythm is viewed as a complete goal.

fi: Tänään ei ole mitään erityistä ohjelmaa.
en: Today there's nothing special planned.
pu: Tänään ei oo mitään erikoista ohjelmaa.
lit: Today not is anything-PART special-PART programme-PART.
note: Negation pulls the whole phrase into the partitive.

en: I work from Monday to Friday.
note: From-to spans use elative + illative: -sta … -hin.

fi: Työaikani on joustava, voin tulla myöhemmin.
en: My working hours are flexible, I can come in later.
pu: Mun työaika on joustava, mä voin tulla myöhemmin.
lit: Work-time-my is flexible, can-I to-come later.
note: liukuva työaika (flexitime) is the standard term in Finnish workplaces.

en: I have a meeting at ten o'clock.
note: palaveri is the everyday word; kokous is more formal.

en: I'll send you the report tomorrow morning.
pu: Mä lähetän sulle raportin huomen aamul.
note: Recipient takes the allative. Total object raportin = the whole report, completed.

fi: Voisitko katsoa tämän läpi ennen kokousta?
en: Could you look this over before the meeting?
pu: Voisiksä kattoo tän läpi ennen kokousta?
lit: Could-you to-look this through before meeting-PART.
note: katsoa läpi = to review. tämän → tän is universal in speech.

en: I'm on sick leave for the rest of the week.
note: States use the adessive: lomalla, sairaslomalla, vuorotteluvapaalla.

en: I'm looking for a new job at the moment.
pu: Mä haen uutta duunii tällä hetkel.
note: hakea takes a partitive object when the search is ongoing.

en: I sent the application and CV yesterday.
pu: Mä lähetin hakemuksen ja cv:n eilen.
note: ansioluettelo = CV. In speech people just say the letters: cv (see-vee).

en: I was invited to an interview next week.
note: In the passive, the personal object takes the special accusative minut, sinut, hänet.

en: The salary is paid on the last day of the month.
note: Passive present + essive for the day. kuukauden shortens to kuun.

en: I work remotely two days a week.
pu: Mä teen etätöitä kaks päivää viikos.
note: etätyö became everyday vocabulary in Finland; the plural partitive etätöitä is the normal form.

en: My supervisor is really understanding.
note: pomo (boss) is the everyday word; esihenkilö is the modern gender-neutral official term.

en: Work is piling up, I can't get to everything.
pu: Duunit kasautuu, mä en ehi kaikkee.
note: ehtiä = to have time to do something. Negation forces the partitive kaikkea.

en: I'm taking a three-week summer holiday in July.
pu: Mä pidän kolmen viikon kesäloman heinäkuus.
note: Measure phrases before a noun go in the genitive: kolmen viikon loma.

en: Shall we set the meeting for Thursday?
note: The translative (-ksi) marks a deadline or target day: torstaiksi = by/for Thursday.

en: I have a lot to do today.
note: paljon always governs the partitive. Both tehtävää and tekemistä work here.

en: Could we push the meeting back by an hour?
note: The adessive expresses the amount of change: tunnilla = by one hour.

en: The employment contract is permanent.
note: toistaiseksi voimassa oleva is the legal phrase; vakituinen is what people actually say.

en: I'm resigning with one month's notice.
note: irtisanoutua = to resign (yourself); irtisanoa = to fire someone. One letter changes everything.

en: Thank you for the good cooperation.
note: A standard closing line in Finnish work emails. kiitos + elative.

en: I study Finnish three times a week.
pu: Mä opiskelen suomee kolme kertaa viikos.
note: kerta after a numeral goes to singular partitive: kertaa.

en: The course starts at the beginning of September.
note: alkaa is intransitive (something begins); aloittaa is transitive (someone starts something).

fi: Kielioppi on vaikeaa, mutta sanasto tulee helpommin.
en: Grammar is hard, but vocabulary comes more easily.
pu: Kielioppi on vaikeeta, mut sanasto tulee helpommin.
lit: Grammar is difficult-PART, but vocabulary comes easier.
note: Abstract subjects take a partitive complement: kielioppi on vaikeaa.

en: I don't understand this word.
note: ymmärtää always takes a partitive object, positive or negative.

en: What does this mean in Finnish?
note: The translative -ksi means 'in a language': suomeksi, englanniksi.

en: Could you write it on the board?
note: Surfaces take the allative -lle for 'onto'.

en: I always do the homework the same evening.
pu: Mä teen kotitehtävät aina samana iltana.
note: The essive -na marks a point in time: samana iltana, ensi vuonna.

en: The exam is next Wednesday.
note: Weekday in the essive; the qualifier ensi viikon in the genitive.

en: I passed the exam with good grades.
pu: Mä pääsin kokeesta läpi hyvin arvosanoin.
note: The instructive plural (-in) is formal; speech prefers päästä kokeesta läpi.

en: Can you explain that again?
note: tuon → ton in speech. uudelleen and uudestaan are interchangeable.

en: I practise pronunciation every day.
note: harjoitella takes a partitive object because practising is never 'complete'.

en: Finnish has fifteen grammatical cases.
note: Numeral + singular partitive: sijamuotoa. The classic fact about Finnish.

en: I read Finnish-language news every morning.
pu: Mä luen suomenkielisii uutisii joka aamu.
note: Plural partitive -ia/-iä. Selkouutiset (easy Finnish news) is the classic learner resource.

en: I can read better than I can speak.
pu: Mä osaan lukee paremmin ku puhuu.
note: kuin ('than') reduces to ku in speech. osata = know how to, opposed to voida = be able to.

en: I need to revise the verb types.
note: Finnish verbs fall into six types; knowing which type a verb is tells you its stem.

en: The teacher gave us a lot of feedback.
note: ope is the affectionate everyday short form of opettaja.

en: It's quiet and peaceful in the library.
note: Impersonal 'it is' + adjective always takes the partitive.

en: I borrowed three books with my library card.
note: Instrument = adessive -lla/-llä. Finnish libraries are free and excellent for learners.

en: I'm taking the YKI test at the intermediate level.
note: YKI keskitaso corresponds to B1 and is the level required for Finnish citizenship.

fi: Mitä enemmän puhun, sitä paremmin opin.
en: The more I speak, the better I learn.
pu: Mitä enemmän mä puhun, sitä paremmin mä opin.
lit: What more speak-I, that better learn-I.
note: mitä … sitä + comparative is the Finnish 'the more … the more' structure.

en: What shall we make for dinner today?
note: laittaa ruokaa = to cook. The translative -ksi marks the intended result.

en: I'm boiling potatoes and frying fish.
pu: Mä keitän perunoita ja paistan kalaa.
note: Both objects are partitive: the cooking is still in progress.

en: Do you have any food allergies?
note: Yes/no questions about existence use a plural partitive for indefinite quantity.

en: I'm a vegetarian, I don't eat meat.
pu: Mä oon kasvissyöjä, mä en syö lihaa.
note: Negation forces the partitive object lihaa.

fi: Tämä resepti on todella helppo ja nopea.
en: This recipe is really easy and quick.
pu: Tää resepti on tosi helppo ja nopee.
lit: This recipe is really easy and quick.
note: todella / tosi both mean 'really'; tosi is the spoken default.

fi: Lisää suolaa ja pippuria maun mukaan.
en: Add salt and pepper to taste.
pu: Lisää suolaa ja pippuria maun mukaan.
lit: Add salt-PART and pepper-PART taste-of according.
note: X:n mukaan = according to X, always with the genitive. Standard recipe phrasing.

en: Let it simmer for about a quarter of an hour.
note: antaa jonkun tehdä = let someone/something do. X:n verran = about the amount of X.

en: The food is ready, come and eat!
note: Plural imperative -kaa/-kää. The -maan infinitive follows verbs of motion.

en: This tastes really good.
note: Sense verbs (maistua, tuoksua, näyttää, kuulostaa) take the ablative -lta/-ltä.

en: The food ended up a bit cold.
note: jäädä + translative = to end up in a state.

en: Would you like some more? There's still some in the pan.
note: lisää is the partitive comparative of paljon, used as 'more (of something)'.

fi: Kiitos ruoasta, se oli todella hyvää.
en: Thanks for the meal, it was really good.
pu: Kiitti ruoasta, se oli tosi hyvää.
lit: Thanks food-from, it was really good-PART.
note: Kiitos ruoasta is said after every family meal in Finland. The complement hyvää is partitive.

en: I'll put the leftovers in the fridge for tomorrow.
note: The translative -ksi marks the future point: huomiseksi = for tomorrow.

en: I bake cardamom buns on Sundays.
note: pulla is the Finnish cardamom bun — a cultural institution with coffee.

fi: Meillä on tapana syödä puuroa aamiaiseksi.
en: We usually eat porridge for breakfast.
pu: Meil on tapana syödä puuroo aamiaiseks.
lit: At-us is custom-as to-eat porridge-PART breakfast-for.
note: olla tapana = to be in the habit of. Very natural B1 structure.

fi: Maito on happanut, heitä se pois.
en: The milk has gone sour, throw it away.
pu: Maito on hapantunu, heitä se pois.
lit: Milk is soured, throw it away.
note: heittää pois = to throw away. Imperative singular drops the -n from the stem.

en: Check the expiry date before use.
pu: Tsekkaa viimenen käyttöpäivä ennen ku käytät.
note: Finnish packaging says parasta ennen (best before) or viimeinen käyttöajankohta.

en: Thaw the meat in the fridge overnight.
note: yön yli = overnight. The postposition yli takes the genitive.

en: I like spicy food.
note: tykätä governs the elative -sta/-stä. Both adjective and noun take it.

en: Could you pass the salt?
note: Total object suolan because you want the whole salt shaker handed over.

en: Do you have a free table for two?
note: Number of people takes the allative: kahdelle, kolmelle, neljälle.

en: Could I have the menu, please?
note: Saisinko is the polite conditional — the single most useful ordering word in Finnish.

en: I'll have the soup of the day and some bread.
pu: Mä otan päivän keiton ja leipää.
note: Contrast the two objects: keiton (whole portion) vs leipää (some bread).

en: Does this dish contain gluten?
note: Existential questions put the thing asked about in the partitive.

en: Could this be made without dairy products?
note: ilman always governs the partitive.

en: One large coffee to go, please.
note: mukaan = to take away. The counter phrase every Finnish café understands.

en: Shall we eat here or take it away?
note: vai (not tai) is used in either-or questions.

en: The food was excellent, thank you very much.
pu: Ruoka oli tosi hyvää, kiitti paljon.
note: Mass nouns take a partitive complement: ruoka oli hyvää, not hyvä.

en: Could we have the bill, please?
note: Conditional + -ko is the standard polite request form.

en: Shall we pay together or separately?
note: Splitting the bill is normal in Finland — this question is asked constantly.

en: Can I pay by card?
note: Payment method = adessive: kortilla, käteisellä, puhelimella.

en: I'd like to book a table for Saturday evening.
note: Translative -ksi for the target time slot. haluaisin = polite 'I would like'.

en: Excuse me, I ordered a different dish.
note: eri is indeclinable — it never takes an ending.

fi: Ruoka on vähän kylmää, voisitteko lämmittää sen?
en: The food is a bit cold, could you heat it up?
pu: Ruoka on vähän kylmää, voisitteks lämmittää sen?
lit: Food is a-bit cold-PART, could-you-PL to-heat it-ACC.
note: Use the polite plural te with staff you don't know.

en: Where is the toilet?
note: vessa is the ordinary word — not rude. Formal signs say WC or naiset/miehet.

en: Is a drink included in the lunch price?
note: kuulua + illative = to be included in. Finnish lunch deals usually include drink, salad and bread.

en: I'll have the same as you.
note: sama inflects like a normal noun: saman, samaa, samassa.

en: Would you recommend something local?
note: jotain (partitive of jokin) plus a partitive adjective is the natural pairing.

en: The waiter will come in a moment.
note: X:n päästä = in X amount of time. viiden minuutin päästä = in five minutes.

en: Cheers! Enjoy your meal.
note: Hyvää ruokahalua is the Finnish bon appétit; the reply is Kiitos samoin.

en: I'll go to the shop in the afternoon.
note: käydä kaupassa uses the inessive because you go and come back.

en: I need milk, bread and coffee.
pu: Mä tarviin maitoo, leipää ja kahvii.
note: tarvita always takes a partitive object for uncountable things. tarvitsen → tarviin in speech.

en: Where are the fruits?
note: Plural subject + on is normal in speech, ovat in writing.

en: Is this on offer this week?
note: olla tarjouksessa = to be on sale. Time spans use the adessive: tällä viikolla.

fi: Otan kilon jauhelihaa ja puoli kiloa porkkanoita.
en: I'll take a kilo of minced meat and half a kilo of carrots.
pu: Mä otan kilon jauhelihaa ja puol kiloo porkkanoita.
lit: Take-I kilo-ACC minced-meat-PART and half kilo-PART carrot-PL-PART.
note: The measure word takes the object case; the substance stays partitive.

en: Do you need a bag?
note: Shop staff use the polite plural te. Bags cost extra in Finnish shops.

en: Do you have a loyalty card?
note: Existential questions use the partitive. S-Etukortti and Plussakortti are the two big Finnish loyalty cards.

en: Can I return this without a receipt?
pu: Voinks mä palauttaa tän ilman kuittii?
note: ilman + partitive. Always keep the kuitti — Finnish shops ask for it.

fi: Tämä paita on liian pieni, onko isompaa kokoa?
en: This shirt is too small, do you have a bigger size?
pu: Tää paita on liian pieni, onks isompaa kokoo?
lit: This shirt is too small, is-Q bigger-PART size-PART?
note: Comparative iso → isompi, partitive isompaa.

en: Can I try this on?
note: sovittaa takes a partitive object — trying on is an unfinished action.

en: Where is the fitting room?
note: koppi = booth/cabin, also used in puhelinkoppi (phone booth).

fi: Tämä on liian kallista, etsin halvempaa.
en: This is too expensive, I'm looking for something cheaper.
pu: Tää on liian kallista, mä etin halvempaa.
lit: This is too expensive-PART, seek-I cheaper-PART.
note: halpa → halvempi shows p → v gradation in the comparative.

en: The shop closes at nine in the evening.
note: mennä kiinni is the everyday alternative to sulkeutua.

en: The opening hours are next to the door.
note: vieressä is a postposition and requires the genitive before it.

en: I return the bottles to the deposit machine.
note: Finland's bottle deposit (pantti) system is universal — every shop has a machine.

fi: Voitteko auttaa? En löydä tätä tuotetta.
en: Could you help? I can't find this product.
pu: Voitteks te auttaa? Mä en löydä tätä tuotetta.
lit: Can-you-PL to-help? Not-I find this-PART product-PART.
note: Negation forces the partitive object even for a specific item.

en: I bought these in the sale.
note: Source = elative -sta/-stä. nämä → nää in speech.

en: The product is out of stock.
note: loppua = to run out. The perfect on loppunut describes the current state.

en: Thanks, nothing else this time.
note: tällä kertaa = this time, adessive. Standard closing line at a counter.

en: I'll pay by card, thanks.
note: Instrument = adessive -lla/-llä. Finland is close to cashless.

en: I don't have cash on me.
note: Negative possession takes the partitive: käteinen → käteistä.

en: Can I withdraw money from the ATM?
note: Otto is the brand name of Finland's ATM network, used as a common noun.

en: The bill is due next Friday.
note: eräpäivä (due date) is a word you meet on every Finnish invoice.

en: I paid the bill in online banking.
note: Total object laskun because the payment was completed.

en: There isn't enough money in the account.
note: tarpeeksi always governs the partitive.

en: Could you lend me twenty euros?
note: lainata means both lend and borrow; the allative minulle makes it 'lend'.

en: I'll pay you back on payday.
note: Named days take the essive: palkkapäivänä, syntymäpäivänä.

fi: Hinnat ovat nousseet paljon viime vuonna.
en: Prices have risen a lot over the past year.
pu: Hinnat on noussu paljon viime vuonna.
lit: Prices are risen much last year-as.
note: nousta (to rise) is intransitive; nostaa (to raise) is transitive.

en: I try to save a little every month.
pu: Mä yritän säästää joka kuukaus vähän.
note: joka + nominative singular for 'every': joka kuukausi, joka päivä.

en: Rent takes a big chunk of the salary.
note: osa jostakin = a part of something, with the elative.

en: Could I have the receipt, please?
note: Saanko is direct; Saisinko is the softer conditional.

en: This payment went to the wrong account.
note: Destination of a transfer takes the allative -lle.

en: The price includes VAT.
note: alv is the universal abbreviation; the inflected slang form is alvin.

en: Did you get a refund on your taxes?
note: veronpalautus (tax refund) arrives in Finland in the summer — a national event.

fi: Minulla on liian tiukka budjetti tässä kuussa.
en: My budget is too tight this month.
pu: Mul on liian tiukka budjetti tässä kuussa.
lit: At-me is too tight budget this-in month-in.
note: Time expressions with tässä take the inessive: tässä kuussa.

en: Shall we split the bill in half?
note: puoliksi is a translative adverb: into halves.

en: It's not worth the price.
note: arvoinen requires the genitive before it: rahan arvoinen, hintansa arvoinen.

en: I bought it on installments.
note: Method of payment stays in the adessive, like kortilla and käteisellä.

en: The price is negotiated separately.
note: Passive present -taan/-tään. Speech prefers sopia jostakin (agree about something).

en: I go to work by bus.
note: Means of transport = adessive: bussilla, junalla, autolla, pyörällä.

en: When does the next train leave?
note: lähteä = to depart. Finnish uses the present tense for scheduled future events.

en: The train is ten minutes late.
note: olla myöhässä = to be late (inessive of myöhä).

en: I bought the ticket from the app.
note: äppi is everyday slang for sovellus (app).

en: Do I have to change trains in Tampere?
note: Tampere takes the adessive -lla, one of the cities that behaves this way.

en: Where does bus number seven leave from?
note: Finns nickname bus numbers: seiska (7), kutonen (6), nelonen (4).

en: I'm getting off at the next stop.
note: jäädä pois = to get off. Stops take the adessive.

en: The journey takes about two hours.
note: kestää + duration in the partitive.

en: I booked a flight from Helsinki to Dubai.
note: lento → lennon shows nt → nn gradation.

en: The flight is delayed by two hours.
note: The adessive expresses the size of a delay or change.

en: My suitcase didn't arrive.
note: tulla perille = to arrive at the destination. perille is a fixed allative form.

en: How far is it to the city centre?
note: keskusta takes the illative -aan for movement toward it.

en: Could you order a taxi to the airport?
note: kenttä (field) takes the allative -lle, like most open places.

en: I drive carefully in slippery conditions.
note: keli (road/weather conditions) is a distinctly Finnish concept. ajaa autoa takes a partitive object.

en: Winter tyres have to be changed in October.
note: pitää + infinitive without an explicit subject means 'one must'.

en: The car is at the garage this week.
note: Duration in the accusative: tämän viikon = for this whole week.

en: Parking costs two euros per hour.
note: 'Per' is the ablative: tunnilta, päivältä, kuukaudelta.

en: I got a parking fine yesterday.
note: Officially pysäköintivirhemaksu, but nobody says that out loud.

en: I cycle in summer and walk in winter.
pu: Mä pyöräilen kesäl ja kävelen talvel.
note: Seasons take the adessive: kesällä, talvella, keväällä, syksyllä.

en: Have a good trip and drive safely!
note: Wishes stay in the partitive, since toivotan is understood.

en: Excuse me, where is the nearest pharmacy?
note: lähin is the superlative of lähellä oleva. Apteekki is the only place selling medicine in Finland.

en: Go straight on and turn right.
note: Directions use the allative: oikealle, vasemmalle. Static position uses oikealla.

en: It's over there on the left side.
note: Static location = adessive. Compare vasemmalle (to the left).

fi: Kävele kadun päähän ja käänny risteyksestä.
en: Walk to the end of the street and turn at the junction.
pu: Kävele kadun päähän ja käänny risteyksestä.
lit: Walk street-of end-into and turn junction-from.
note: pää (end) → päähän. Turning off something uses the elative.

en: The bank is next to the post office.
note: Postpositions like vieressä, edessä, takana all take the genitive.

en: The library is on the other side of the square.
note: tori (market square) is at the heart of every Finnish town.

en: Is there a grocery shop nearby?
note: Existential questions take the partitive: ruokakauppaa.

en: I got lost, I don't know where I am.
pu: Mä eksyin, en tiiä missä mä oon.
note: tiedän → tiiän → tiiä in speech, an extremely common contraction.

en: Could you show it to me on the map?
note: Reading from a surface uses the ablative: kartalta, ruudulta, listalta.

en: The city hall is right in front of the railway station.
note: aivan / ihan both mean 'right, completely'; ihan is the spoken default.

en: How long does it take to walk there?
note: sinne = to there (directional), siellä = there (static).

fi: Se on noin viiden minuutin kävelymatkan päässä.
en: It's about a five-minute walk away.
pu: Se on viien minsan kävelymatkan pääs.
lit: It is about five-of minute-of walking-trip-of distance-at.
note: X:n päässä = at a distance of X. Measure phrases take the genitive.

en: The bus stop is on the other side of the road.
note: tie → tien in the genitive, no gradation.

en: Turn left at the second junction.
note: Ordinals inflect fully: toinen, toisen, toisesta.

en: Is there a lift here?
note: Existential questions always use the partitive for the thing sought.

en: Let's go up to the second floor.
note: The passive doubles as the 'let's' form: mennään, tehdään, katsotaan.

en: The entrance is behind the building.
note: takana (static) vs taakse (motion behind) vs takaa (from behind).

fi: Ajoitko sinä ohi? Se jäi taakse.
en: Did you drive past it? It's behind us now.
note: ajaa ohi = to drive past. taakse marks movement to behind.

en: This street is one-way.
note: Adjectives ending in -inen lose the i in speech: yksisuuntainen → yksisuuntanen.

en: Thanks for the help, I'll find my way there.
pu: Kiitti avusta, mä löydän kyl perille.
note: kyllä here is an emphasis particle, not an answer to a question.

en: The weather is beautiful today.
note: sää = weather in general; ilma can also mean weather as well as air.

en: It's raining outside.
note: sataa always needs an object: sataa vettä (rain), sataa lunta (snow), sataa rakeita (hail).

en: Tomorrow it will snow all day.
note: koko päivän is an accusative of duration: for the whole day.

en: It's cold, put a coat on.
note: pukea päälle = to put on. Imperative singular is the bare verb stem.

en: The temperature will drop to minus ten degrees.
note: pakkanen = frost / sub-zero. X astetta pakkasta is how Finns say minus X.

fi: Tuulee kovaa ja on hyvin kosteaa.
en: It's windy and very damp.
pu: Tuulee kovaa ja on tosi kosteeta.
lit: Winds hard-PART and is very damp-PART.
note: Weather verbs are impersonal: tuulee, sataa, paistaa — no subject at all.

en: The sun is shining, let's go outside.
note: ulos (motion out) vs ulkona (static outside) vs ulkoa (from outside).

fi: Kesällä aurinko ei laske ollenkaan pohjoisessa.
en: In summer the sun doesn't set at all in the north.
pu: Kesäl aurinko ei laske ollenkaan pohjosessa.
lit: Summer-on sun not sets at-all north-in.
note: The midnight sun (yötön yö) is a Lapland phenomenon.

en: In winter it's dark already at four.
note: Impersonal 'it is' + adjective takes the partitive: pimeää, valoisaa.

en: The polar night lasts many weeks in Lapland.
note: monta always takes a singular partitive after it: monta viikkoa.

en: The roads are slippery, be careful.
note: Plural subject + plural partitive complement. ole → oo in speech.

en: The forecast promises dry weather for the weekend.
note: pouta = dry weather with no rain. A word Finnish weather reports love.

en: Take an umbrella with you.
note: mukaan = along with you (directional); mukana = with you (static).

en: In autumn the foliage colours are really beautiful.
note: ruska has no English equivalent — the autumn colours of northern Finland.

en: The lake is frozen from December to April.
note: olla jäässä = to be frozen over. Time span: elative → illative.

en: Spring is coming late this year.
note: tänä vuonna uses the essive; contrast tässä kuussa (inessive).

en: The weather will warm up next week.
note: lämmetä → lämpenee. Intransitive: it warms by itself; lämmittää would be transitive.

en: Thunder is rumbling in the distance.
note: kaukana (static, far away) vs kauas (to far away) vs kaukaa (from far).

en: What's the weather like tomorrow?
note: millainen → millanen in speech, along with all -lainen words.

fi: Ei ole huonoa säätä, on vain huonoja vaatteita.
en: There's no bad weather, only bad clothing.
pu: Ei oo huonoo säätä, on vaan huonoja vaatteita.
lit: Not is bad-PART weather-PART, is only bad-PL-PART clothes-PL-PART.
note: A Nordic proverb every Finn knows. Note the negative partitive throughout.

en: I have a fever and a headache.
note: Symptoms are always partitive: kuumetta, kipua, yskää.

en: My throat is sore.
note: kipeä → kipee is one of the most recognisable puhekieli vowel changes.

en: I'd like to book an appointment with the doctor.
note: varata aika = to book an appointment, literally 'to reserve a time'.

fi: Onko teillä vapaita aikoja tällä viikolla?
en: Do you have any free appointments this week?
pu: Onks teil vapaita aikoja tällä viikolla?
lit: Is-Q at-you free-PL-PART time-PL-PART this-at week-at.
note: Plural partitive for an indefinite quantity of appointments.

en: The symptoms started three days ago.
note: X sitten = X ago, with the time in the partitive.

en: It hurts me right here.
note: särkeä is impersonal and takes the experiencer in the partitive: minua särkee.

en: I take painkillers for the headache.
note: Medicine for a condition uses the illative. Burana is the ibuprofen brand Finns name by default.

en: The doctor wrote me a prescription.
note: Recipient = allative. Finnish prescriptions are electronic (sähköinen resepti).

fi: Ota lääke kahdesti päivässä ruoan kanssa.
en: Take the medicine twice a day with food.
pu: Ota lääke kahesti päiväs ruoan kaa.
lit: Take medicine twice day-in food-of with.
note: Frequency per unit uses the inessive: kolmesti viikossa, kerran kuussa.

en: I'm allergic to penicillin.
note: allerginen governs the allative -lle. Essential to know at a doctor's.

en: I'm going to the health centre in the morning.
note: terkkari is the everyday slang for terveyskeskus.

en: I need a sick leave certificate for my employer.
note: In Finland you usually need a certificate after three days of illness.

en: My ankle is sprained.
note: Perfect participle -nyt describes a resulting state. Speech drops the final -t.

en: My blood pressure is slightly elevated.
note: olla koholla = to be raised, a fixed adessive expression.

fi: Minun pitäisi liikkua enemmän ja nukkua paremmin.
en: I should exercise more and sleep better.
pu: Mun pitäis liikkuu enemmän ja nukkuu paremmin.
lit: My should to-move more and to-sleep better.
note: liikkua = to be physically active, the everyday Finnish word for exercise.

en: You'll surely get better soon.
note: parantua/parata = to recover. A standard well-wish.

en: Get well soon!
note: A fixed partitive wish, like Hyvää matkaa and Onnea.

en: The dentist removed the wisdom tooth.
note: hammas → hampaan shows the mm/mp gradation pattern.

en: Call the emergency number 112.
note: soittaa + illative for a number called. 112 works throughout the EU.

en: Kela reimburses part of the medicine costs.
note: Kela is Finland's social insurance institution — an unavoidable word here.

en: I go to the gym three times a week.
pu: Mä käyn salil kolme kertaa viikos.
note: sali (gym) takes the adessive -lla. Frequency per unit uses the inessive.

en: I play football every Saturday.
note: pelata takes a partitive object. futis is the universal slang for jalkapallo.

en: I started running last spring.
note: The -minen noun turns a verb into a thing: juosta → juokseminen.

fi: Juoksen viisi kilometriä kolme kertaa viikossa.
en: I run five kilometres three times a week.
pu: Mä juoksen viis kilsaa kolme kertaa viikos.
lit: Run-I five kilometre-PART three time-PART week-in.
note: kilsa is everyday slang for kilometri.

en: Skiing is popular in winter.
note: An abstract subject takes a partitive complement: suosittua, not suosittu.

en: I went swimming at the swimming pool.
note: käydä + -massa/-mässä = went and did something and came back.

en: My muscles are sore after the workout.
note: jälkeen is a postposition taking the genitive. treeni is universal gym slang.

en: Always stretch after training.
note: Imperative of a -ella verb: venytellä → venyttele.

en: I injured my knee during the game.
note: X:n aikana = during X, always with the genitive.

en: The team won the match two-one.
note: matsi is a loan from English 'match' and completely standard in speech.

en: Ice hockey is Finland's national sport.
note: lätkä is the affectionate slang name for jääkiekko.

en: I'll watch the match on TV in the evening.
note: Watching from a screen uses the elative: televisiosta, netistä.

en: I always cheer for my own team.
pu: Mä kannustan aina mun omaa joukkuetta.
note: kannustaa takes a partitive object for continuous support.

en: My fitness has improved considerably.
note: kunto = physical condition; hyvässä kunnossa = in good shape.

en: I walk up the stairs instead of the lift.
pu: Mä kävelen portaat ylös hissin sijaan.
note: X:n sijaan = instead of X, with the genitive.

en: I'm taking part in a marathon next spring.
note: osallistua governs the illative or allative depending on the event.

en: Without a proper warm-up you'll get injured easily.
pu: Ilman kunnon lämmittelyy sä loukkaannut helposti.
note: ilman + partitive. The 2nd person singular here is generic 'one'.

en: In summers I jog on the forest path.
note: lenkkeillä = to go for a jog/walk. The -isin suffix marks habitual seasons.

en: I need new running shoes.
note: lenkkarit (trainers) is plural like most footwear words.

en: Exercise helps you cope with everyday life.
note: jaksaa = to have the energy to. auttaa + -maan infinitive.

en: My hobbies are photography and reading.
note: harrastaa takes a partitive object and has no neat English equivalent.

en: In my free time I listen to music.
note: musa is the everyday slang for musiikki.

fi: Soitan kitaraa, mutta en kovin hyvin.
en: I play the guitar, but not very well.
pu: Mä soitan kitaraa, mut en kovin hyvin.
lit: Play-I guitar-PART, but not-I very well.
note: soittaa = to play an instrument; pelata = to play a game. Never mix them.

en: I go to choir on Wednesday evenings.
note: The -isin suffix stacks onto compounds: keskiviikkoiltaisin.

en: I read that book in a single evening.
pu: Mä luin sen kirjan yhes illas.
note: Total object kirjan because the reading was completed.

en: I'm reading that book right now.
pu: Mä luen sitä kirjaa just nyt.
note: Compare with the previous sentence: partitive object = action still ongoing.

en: We went to the cinema last Friday.
note: elokuvissa is plural inessive. leffa is the slang for elokuva.

en: That film was really touching.
note: Participles used as adjectives: koskettava, jännittävä, kiinnostava.

en: I prefer documentaries to action films.
pu: Mä tykkään enemmän dokkareista ku toimintaleffoista.
note: pitää jostakin + enemmän kuin = to prefer. Both nouns take the elative.

en: I spend too much time on my phone.
note: viettää aikaa = to spend time. liikaa always governs the partitive.

en: I took up a new hobby in the autumn.
note: Total object because the starting is a completed act.

fi: Marjastus ja sienestys ovat suomalaisia perinteitä.
en: Berry picking and mushroom foraging are Finnish traditions.
pu: Marjastus ja sienestys on suomalaisii perinteitä.
lit: Berry-picking and mushrooming are Finnish-PL-PART tradition-PL-PART.
note: Everyman's rights (jokamiehenoikeudet) let anyone pick berries in any forest.

en: I go to the summer cottage every summer.
note: mökki (summer cottage) takes the adessive -llä. A central Finnish institution.

en: Fishing calms the mind.
note: rauhoittaa takes a partitive object for a continuous effect.

en: I play board games with friends.
note: kanssa needs the genitive. kaveri is the warm everyday word for ystävä.

en: I paint pictures on weekends.
note: Plural partitive object: an indefinite number of paintings.

en: Handicrafts are a relaxing hobby.
note: Knitting (neulominen) is a genuinely mainstream Finnish pastime.

en: I don't have time for hobbies.
note: Negative existential takes the partitive aikaa; the beneficiary takes the allative.

en: What do you most like doing in your free time?
note: mieluiten is the superlative of mielellään: most gladly.

en: Let's go on a hike next Sunday.
note: The passive doubles as 'let's'. retki (excursion) takes the allative.

en: What time is it?
note: Also Mitä kello on? Both are equally standard.

en: It's a quarter to three.
note: vaille = to (before the hour); yli = past. varttia vaille kolme = 2:45.

en: It's ten past seven.
note: The minutes take the partitive before yli and vaille.

en: Let's meet at six o'clock in the centre.
note: kello kuusi (nominative) or kuudelta (ablative) — both mean 'at six'.

en: I'm about fifteen minutes late.
note: vartti = a quarter of an hour. The accusative marks the extent of lateness.

en: Can you make it half an hour earlier?
note: ehtiä = to have enough time to do something.

en: See you next week.
note: Time spans use the adessive: tällä viikolla, ensi viikolla, viime viikolla.

en: Does Thursday or Friday suit you?
note: sopia + allative for the person. vai for either-or questions.

fi: Minulla on jo menoa siihen aikaan.
en: I already have something on at that time.
pu: Mul on jo menoa siihen aikaan.
lit: At-me is already going-PART that-into time-into.
note: olla menoa = to have plans/commitments. siihen aikaan = at that time.

en: Shall we move the meeting to next week?
note: Moving to a future point uses the illative: ensi viikkoon, ensi kuuhun.

en: I'll get back to you on this tomorrow.
note: palata asiaan is standard business Finnish for 'I'll follow up'.

en: The day before yesterday it rained all day.
note: toissapäivänä (day before yesterday), ylihuomenna (day after tomorrow).

en: The day after tomorrow is Midsummer Eve.
note: Juhannus is the biggest summer holiday in Finland; cities empty out.

en: There's still plenty of time.
note: Quantity adverbs like runsaasti and vähän force the partitive.

fi: Deadline on ensi kuun ensimmäinen päivä.
en: The deadline is the first day of next month.
pu: Deadline on ens kuun eka päivä.
lit: Deadline is next month-of first day.
note: eka is the everyday spoken form of ensimmäinen; toka = toinen.

en: Wait a moment, I'll be right there.
note: odota → oota is one of the most frequent speech reductions.

fi: Ennen kuin lähdet, muista lukita ovi.
en: Before you leave, remember to lock the door.
pu: Ennen ku lähet, muista lukita ovi.
lit: Before than leave-you, remember to-lock door.
note: ennen kuin introduces a clause; plain ennen takes a noun in the partitive.

fi: Sen jälkeen kun muutin, kaikki on ollut helpompaa.
en: Since I moved, everything has been easier.
pu: Sen jälkeen ku mä muutin, kaikki on ollu helpompaa.
lit: That-of after when moved-I, everything is been easier-PART.
note: sen jälkeen kun = after/since, followed by a full clause.

en: I've been here since the morning.
pu: Mä oon ollu täällä aamust asti.
note: X:sta asti = since X, with the elative.

fi: Aika kuluu nopeasti, kun on kiireinen.
en: Time passes quickly when you're busy.
pu: Aika kuluu nopeesti, ku on kiire.
lit: Time passes quickly, when is busy.
note: kulua = to pass/elapse. Subjectless clauses express a general truth.

en: Can I call you later?
note: soittaa + allative for the person you call.

en: What's your phone number?
note: In speech the possessive suffix is dropped and sun carries the meaning.

en: I tried to call, but you didn't answer.
pu: Mä yritin soittaa, mut sä et vastannu.
note: Negative past: et + past participle vastannut. Speech drops the final -t.

en: My phone battery is dead.
note: kännykkä is the everyday word for mobile phone; olla lopussa = to be out.

en: I'll send you a message in the evening.
note: laittaa viesti is far more common in speech than lähettää viesti.

fi: En kuule sinua, kuuluvuus on huono.
en: I can't hear you, the reception is bad.
pu: Mä en kuule sua, kuuluvuus on huono.
lit: Not-I hear you-PART, reception is bad.
note: kuulla takes a partitive object for people. kuuluvuus = signal reception.

en: I'll call back in five minutes.
pu: Mä soitan takas viiden minuutin päästä.
note: X:n päästä = in X amount of time. takaisin → takas in speech.

en: The call cut off halfway.
note: katketa = to break off (intransitive); katkaista = to cut off (transitive).

en: Leave a message on the voicemail.
note: vastaaja = answering machine, from vastata (to answer).

en: The phone is on silent for the duration of the meeting.
note: olla äänettömällä = to be on silent. X:n ajan = for the duration of X.

en: I'll send you the address by text message.
note: tekstari is the slang for tekstiviesti. Means of sending = adessive.

en: Did you see my message yesterday?
note: näitkö → näitsä: the -tkö ending fuses with sinä in speech.

en: I'll reply as soon as I have time.
pu: Mä vastaan sulle heti ku mä ehin.
note: heti kun = as soon as. vastata + allative for the person.

en: The number is wrong, I dialled incorrectly.
pu: Numero on väärä, mä valitsin väärin.
note: valita = to choose/dial. väärä (adjective) vs väärin (adverb).

en: Could you call me back?
note: minulle → mulle. Puhekieli halves the length of almost every pronoun.

en: The phone is tied to a contract.
note: liittymä = mobile subscription, a word you meet in every Finnish phone shop.

fi: Soitanko sinulle vai soitatko sinä minulle?
en: Shall I call you or will you call me?
pu: Soitanks mä sulle vai soitaksä mulle?
note: vai for genuine either-or questions, never tai.

en: The call costs the normal subscription rate.
note: Total object because the whole fee is charged.

fi: Estin sen numeron, se oli huijaussoitto.
en: I blocked that number, it was a scam call.
pu: Mä estin sen numeron, se oli huijaussoitto.
lit: Blocked-I that-ACC number-ACC, it was scam-call.
note: estää = to block/prevent. huijaus = fraud, scam.

en: Goodbye and thanks for calling.
note: Kuulemiin is the phone-specific goodbye; Näkemiin is for face to face.

en: What's the wifi password?
note: Foreign words still inflect: wifi → wifin in the genitive.

en: The internet connection is really slow today.
note: netti (internet) is fully naturalised Finnish now.

en: My computer crashed in the middle of work.
note: kaatua = to crash (of a computer), literally 'to fall over'. kone = machine, i.e. computer.

en: You did remember to save the file, right?
note: The clitic -han softens a question into a gentle reminder.

en: I'll send it to you by email.
note: meili is the spoken form; sähköposti is the written standard.

fi: Salasana pitää vaihtaa kolmen kuukauden välein.
en: The password has to be changed every three months.
pu: Salasana pitää vaihtaa kolmen kuukauden välein.
lit: Password must to-change three-of month-of interval-by.
note: X:n välein = at intervals of X, with the genitive.

en: I forgot my password, I need to reset it.
pu: Mä unohin salasanan, pitää nollata se.
note: nollata = to reset, from nolla (zero).

en: Update the app to the latest version.
note: Superlative uusin → uusimpaan in the illative.

fi: Latasin tiedoston, mutta se ei aukea.
en: I downloaded the file, but it won't open.
pu: Mä latasin tiedoston, mut se ei aukee.
lit: Downloaded-I file-ACC, but it not opens.
note: ladata covers both download and charge (a battery).

en: I save everything to the cloud.
note: kaikki → kaiken as a total object.

en: I use two-factor authentication.
note: käyttää always takes a partitive object.

en: I identify myself with my online banking credentials.
note: pankkitunnukset are the universal Finnish digital ID — used for everything official.

fi: Näyttö on rikki, siinä on halkeama.
en: The screen is broken, there's a crack in it.
pu: Näyttö on rikki, siin on halkeema.
lit: Screen is broken, it-in is crack.
note: rikki is an indeclinable adverb: olla rikki = to be broken.

en: Restart the device.
note: The classic IT instruction. Also uudelleenkäynnistä as a single word.

en: I back up the data every week.
note: varmuuskopio = backup copy, from varma (certain).

en: I follow him on social media.
note: some is the standard Finnish abbreviation for social media. Speech uses se for people.

en: I got some strange spam yesterday.
note: Indefinite quantity takes the partitive: outoa roskapostia.

en: Don't click suspicious links.
note: Negative imperative älä + verb stem. The object goes plural partitive.

en: I look for instructions online.
note: Source = elative. etsiä takes a partitive object for an open-ended search.

en: AI helps with translation.
note: tekoäly literally = 'made intelligence'. auttaa + inessive for the area of help.

en: I'm really tired today.
note: Past participles as adjectives drop the final -t in speech: väsynyt → väsyny.

en: I'm a bit annoyed.
note: Emotion verbs like harmittaa, pelottaa, väsyttää put the experiencer in the partitive.

en: I'm nervous about tomorrow's interview.
note: jännittää covers both nervousness and excitement — context decides.

en: I'm really happy for you.
pu: Mä oon tosi iloinen sun puolesta.
note: jonkun puolesta = on someone's behalf / for someone.

en: In my opinion it was a good decision.
pu: Mun mielestä se oli hyvä päätös.
note: mielestäni / minun mielestäni both work. Speech says mun mielestä.

en: I agree with you.
pu: Mä oon samaa mieltä sun kaa.
note: olla samaa mieltä = to agree; olla eri mieltä = to disagree.

en: I disagree about that matter.
pu: Mä oon eri mieltä tost asiasta.
note: eri never inflects. The topic takes the elative.

en: I'm not sure about that.
note: varma jostakin = sure about something, with the elative.

en: That sounds like a good idea.
note: kuulostaa, näyttää, tuntua and maistua all take the ablative -lta/-ltä.

fi: Tuntuu siltä, että kaikki menee hyvin.
en: It feels like everything is going well.
pu: Tuntuu siltä, et kaikki menee hyvin.
lit: Feels that-from, that everything goes well.
note: tuntuu siltä että = it feels like. että → et in speech.

en: I'm disappointed with the result.
note: pettynyt governs the illative: pettynyt johonkin.

en: I'm afraid to go there alone.
note: pelottaa is impersonal; the person feeling fear is a partitive object.

en: I'm proud of you.
note: ylpeä jostakusta takes the elative. ylpeä → ylpee in speech.

en: I miss my family a lot.
note: kaivata takes a partitive object. Add the possessive suffix in writing.

en: I'm worried about his health.
note: olla huolissaan jostakin. In speech hän becomes se, even for people.

en: I miss you.
note: The warmest way to say 'I miss you' in Finnish. Object stays partitive.

en: That annoys me a great deal.
note: ärsyttää takes a partitive object for the person affected.

en: Hopefully everything will work out.
note: järjestyä = to sort itself out. A very common Finnish reassurance.

en: To be honest, I don't know.
note: A passive participle in the essive works as a discourse marker.

en: What do you think about this?
note: Mitä mieltä olet? is the standard way to ask for an opinion.

en: What are you doing next weekend?
note: Named time units take the essive: viikonloppuna, jouluna, kesänä.

en: Do you want to come along for a coffee?
note: mennä kahville uses the allative — the classic Finnish social invitation.

en: We have plans for Saturday.
note: Indefinite plural takes the partitive; the target day takes the translative.

en: Would you like to come to our place to eat?
note: Conditional -isi- makes the invitation polite rather than demanding.

en: Does six o'clock suit you?
note: sopia takes the allative for the person it suits.

en: Unfortunately I can't make it.
note: päästä = to be able to get somewhere, distinct from voida (to be permitted).

en: Could we move it to another day?
note: Moving to a time point uses the illative.

en: Let me know if the plans change.
note: ilmoittaa + allative. muuttua = to change (intransitive); muuttaa = to change something.

en: Shall we go to the cinema in the evening?
note: The passive + -ko is the standard 'shall we?' construction.

en: I'm inviting you to my birthday party.
note: Personal pronouns have a special accusative: sinut, minut, hänet.

en: The party starts at eight.
note: juhlat is always plural. bileet is the slang equivalent.

en: I'll bring something to drink.
note: The passive participle juotava = drinkable/something to drink.

en: Shall we meet at the square or at the station?
note: Both tori and asema take the adessive -lla.

en: Let's agree on a more exact time later.
note: Comparative tarkka → tarkempi with kk → k gradation.

en: Would you have time on Wednesday?
note: olisiko contracts dramatically in speech: oisko.

en: We're planning a trip to Lapland.
note: Partitive object because the planning is still in progress.

en: I booked the accommodation in advance already.
note: Total object because the booking is complete.

en: Let's take it easy this weekend.
note: ottaa rennosti = to take it easy. rennosti from rento (relaxed).

en: Thanks for the invitation, I'll gladly join.
pu: Kiitti kutsusta, mä tuun mielelläni mukaan.
note: A complete, natural acceptance in one line.

en: Let's see closer to the time.
note: A very Finnish way to avoid committing. sitten → sit in speech.

en: Sorry, that was my fault.
note: sori is the common spoken borrowing; anteeksi is the standard word.

en: I apologise for being late.
note: pahoitella is the formal apology verb, used in emails and at work.

en: I didn't mean it that way.
note: Negative past: en + tarkoittanut. Speech drops the -t and the oi shortens.

en: It was a misunderstanding.
note: A compound of väärin (wrongly) + käsitys (conception).

en: I'd like to make a complaint.
note: tehdä valitus / reklamaatio. The conditional keeps it civil.

en: The product was already faulty when purchased.
pu: Tuote oli viallinen jo ku mä ostin sen.
note: The temporal construction -ttaessa means 'when [it was] being done'.

en: Could you fix this error?
note: Polite plural te when addressing a company or a stranger.

en: I'm still waiting for a reply to my message.
pu: Mä odotan yhä vastausta mun viestiin.
note: odottaa takes a partitive object. vastaus + illative for what it answers.

fi: Tämä ei ole sitä mitä tilasin.
en: This isn't what I ordered.
pu: Tää ei oo sitä mitä mä tilasin.
lit: This not is that-PART what ordered-I.
note: Negation forces the partitive sitä. A relative clause follows with mitä.

en: I want a refund.
note: rahat is plural here — the specific sum paid. Direct but not rude.

en: Who can I complain to about this?
note: valittaa + allative for the person, elative for the topic.

en: The matter is still unresolved.
note: The abessive third infinitive -matta/-mättä means 'without being done'.

en: It wasn't intentional.
note: Negative sentences pull the complement into the partitive.

en: Sorry to bother you.
note: anteeksi että + clause. vaivata takes a partitive object.

fi: Ei se mitään, unohda koko juttu.
en: It's nothing, forget the whole thing.
pu: Ei se mitään, unohda koko juttu.
lit: Not it anything-PART, forget whole thing.
note: Ei se mitään is the standard way to accept an apology.

fi: Yritin parhaani, mutta se ei riittänyt.
en: I did my best, but it wasn't enough.
pu: Mä yritin parhaani, mut se ei riittäny.
lit: Tried-I best-my, but it not sufficed.
note: yrittää parhaansa = to try one's best; the possessive suffix agrees with the subject.

en: We need to talk about this honestly.
note: puhua jostakin = to speak about something, with the elative.

en: Might there be some solution to this?
note: The clitic -han/-hän added to the conditional softens it further still.

en: No worries, I'll handle it.
note: Ei hätää is the everyday Finnish 'no worries'.

en: Thank you for your understanding and patience.
note: kiitos + elative. A standard closing in Finnish customer service messages.

en: I have to go to the register office.
note: Since 2020 the maistraatti is officially DVV (Digi- ja väestötietovirasto).

en: I applied for housing benefit from Kela.
note: hakea + partitive object, source in the elative.

en: The application is still being processed.
note: olla käsittelyssä = to be under processing, a phrase every Kela letter uses.

en: I need a certificate of Finnish language proficiency.
pu: Mä tarviin todistuksen suomen kielen taidosta.
note: todistus jostakin = a certificate of something, with the elative.

en: My residence permit expires next year.
note: umpeutua = to expire. Migri (Maahanmuuttovirasto) handles permits.

en: I booked the appointment online.
note: verkossa is the written standard; netissä is what people actually say.

en: Bring your passport and residence permit card.
note: ottaa mukaan = to bring along. Finnish omits 'your' — context is enough.

en: I reported the move to the post office and to DVV.
pu: Mä ilmotin muutosta postille ja DVV:lle.
note: muuttoilmoitus is mandatory in Finland within a week of moving.

en: The form must be filled in carefully.
note: pitää + infinitive with no subject = a general obligation.

en: Attach a copy of your passport to the application.
note: liittää + illative for the destination, elative for the source document.

fi: Päätös tulee postitse kahden viikon kuluessa.
en: The decision will come by post within two weeks.
pu: Päätös tulee postissa parin viikon sisällä.
lit: Decision comes by-post two-of week-of within.
note: postitse is a prolative form meaning 'via post'. X:n kuluessa = within X.

en: You can handle the matter electronically.
note: hoitaa asia = to take care of a matter. Finland runs almost everything online.

en: I'll take a queue number and wait.
note: vuoronumero is the ticket-queue system used in every Finnish office.

en: Where is the information desk?
note: neuvonta = advisory service, from neuvoa (to advise).

en: I registered as a jobseeker at the employment office.
note: The translative -ksi marks the role you register as.

en: I got a letter from the tax office.
note: Source from a person or institution = ablative -lta/-ltä.

en: Do you need an interpreter for the visit?
note: Public services in Finland provide interpreters free of charge in many cases.

en: The integration training lasts about a year.
note: kotoutuminen (integration) is a key term in Finnish immigration policy.

en: I applied for Finnish citizenship last spring.
pu: Mä hain Suomen kansalaisuutta viime keväänä.
note: Partitive object because the outcome is not yet complete.

en: Thanks, I got all the information I needed.
pu: Kiitos, mä sain kaiken tiedon mitä tarvisin.
note: The agent participle tarvitsemani = 'that I need', a compact B1 structure.

en: Shall we go to the sauna in the evening?
note: Finland has more saunas than cars. sauna takes the illative for going in.

fi: Sauna on lämmin, löyly on hyvä.
en: The sauna is warm, the steam is good.
pu: Sauna on lämmin, löyly on hyvä.
lit: Sauna is warm, steam is good.
note: löyly means the steam that rises when water hits the stones — untranslatable.

en: Throw a bit more water on the stones.
note: heittää löylyä is the fixed phrase; you never 'pour' it in Finnish.

en: I swim in the lake after the sauna.
note: jälkeen takes the genitive. Finland has 188,000 lakes.

en: In winter we go ice swimming.
note: avanto = a hole cut in lake ice. avantouinti is a national pastime.

en: The forest is an important place for Finns.
note: Beneficiary takes the allative -lle. Over 70% of Finland is forest.

en: I pick blueberries in August.
note: Plural partitive object for an indefinite quantity of berries.

en: Everyman's rights allow moving freely in nature.
note: A cornerstone of Finnish life: you may walk, camp and pick berries almost anywhere.

en: At Midsummer people burn a bonfire.
note: The passive expresses 'people do'. kokko = the Midsummer bonfire.

en: Independence Day is celebrated on the sixth of December.
note: Ordinal in the essive for a date. Finns watch the Presidential ball on TV.

en: May Day is students' biggest celebration.
note: Superlative suuri → suurin. Vappu on 1 May fills every Finnish city.

en: Sisu means perseverance in the face of difficulties.
note: sisu is the most famous untranslatable Finnish word. edessä takes the genitive.

en: Finns appreciate silence.
note: arvostaa takes a partitive object. Silence in conversation is comfortable here.

en: Finland drinks the most coffee in the world.
note: eniten is the superlative of paljon. Around 10 kg per person per year.

en: In winter the northern lights are visible in the north.
note: revontulet literally means 'fox fires', from an old Sámi-influenced folk tale.

en: There's no running water at the summer cottage.
note: Negative existential takes the partitive throughout.

en: Finns rarely greet strangers.
note: It isn't unfriendliness — personal space is simply valued differently here.

en: The Kalevala is Finland's national epic.
note: Compiled by Elias Lönnrot in the 1800s from oral poetry; it shaped Finnish identity.

en: Finland is the happiest country in the world.
note: Superlative onnellinen → onnellisin. A statement Finns themselves find amusing.

fi: Ei ole huonoa säätä, on vain huonoa asennetta.
en: There's no bad weather, only a bad attitude.
pu: Ei oo huonoo säätä, on vaan huonoo asennetta.
lit: Not is bad-PART weather-PART, is only bad-PART attitude-PART.
note: A Finnish twist on the old proverb — a fitting last line for a learner's first 500.
